title: Trying On Zen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett recites Mary Oliver's "Wild Geese," then tells how arriving at Green Gulch Farm at 21 felt like trying on a new suit of clothes that might not fit. Norman Fischer taps Nomon's shoulder in a lunch line to ask about staying, and later mentions that he is about to start teaching near Vancouver, just as Nomon heads to Washington State. A note in a Bellingham bookstore leads to a small sitting group, and then to Jukai in a garden in 1993, where Nomon receives a name taken from a seal made in China for Norman. Nomon ends by describing how Norman simplified the ceremony forms and suggests calling the ceremony a "precepts remembering ceremony."

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
I'm pretty sure I first heard this poem by Mary Oliver from Norman many years ago.
It continues to be a poem that I think about and share and recite all over the place.
I got a little tired of it for a while, and then I used it a bunch and people were so moved.
Some things are so timeless.
So, "Wild Geese" by Mary Oliver.
You know this poem?
*You don't have to be good.
You don't have to walk on your knees through the desert for a hundred miles repenting.
You only have to let the soft animal of your body love what it loves.
Tell me about despair, yours, and I will tell you mine.
Meanwhile, the world goes on.
Meanwhile, the sun and the clear pebbles of the rain are moving across the landscapes, over the prairies and the deep trees, the mountains and the rivers.
Meanwhile, the wild geese, high in the clean blue air, are heading home again.
Whoever you are, no matter how lonely, the world offers itself to your imagination.
Calls to you like the wild geese, harsh and exciting, over and over announcing your place in the family of things.*
So anyway, 30 years ago, right now, some earlier version of me.
The more you think about a statement like that, the more suspect it is, don't you think?
Was that really me?
Seems like it was me.
Anyway, we don't want to waste too much time on that.
If you can actually tell the story, we'll say it was me.
I was at Green Gulch Farm, about a month or maybe three weeks into the first residential training period that I sat there.
I was 21 years old.
The head teacher for the practice period was Dainin Katagiri Roshi.
He wasn't there the whole time though.
He came and went a bit.
I think he was also taking care of his sangha in Minnesota at the same time somehow.
Tenshin Reb Anderson was like the teacher on the ground that we saw every day.
There were a group of, I don't know, 15, 16 practice period students, and we were mostly all pretty young.
I'm still in touch with a few of those people, lifelong friends.
And so we went here and went there, and got up and sat zazen and went to classes and did everything.
Norman Fischer was the director of Green Gulch, and he would come and go a bit, interacting with us formally.
I think just one evening a week he taught a class.
I can't remember if it was on the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 lines or if it was on the Genjokoan.
Genjokoan, thanks.
I thought you might remember.
I did two different practice periods and they blend together in my mind.
But Reb appeared somewhere in there.
And I was really pretty impressed by all these great, worthy practitioners.
I didn't really know their stories, but it seemed like they must have been doing this forever.
Very dignified.
Reb Anderson in particular, then and now and probably until the day he dies, has this incredible grace and sort of shininess.
It just kind of floats around through the space.
Later on I had some judgmental feelings about that, but I was also so impressed.
As one does, right?
Norman was a little more ordinary looking, crooked nose, a little galumpy.
So I was a little more comfortable with that.
I went to see, so this is not particularly in order.
If I were to tell the whole story in order, we don't have enough time.
But just impressions.
I went to see Norman towards the end of that first practice period.
In practice discussion, he hadn't yet received Dharma transmission.
So it's called practice discussion, just like it is here, when the teacher is not fully ordained yet.
Are you hearing me okay?
I'm not feeling like talking really loud.
You hear me okay?
No?
Not so much?
You want to move up, Linda?
I'll try to speak up a little bit.
Anyway, I was so surprised at the end of this final interview.
I forget where I was going next.
Norman said, well, I really appreciated practicing with you.
And I think I just said, thanks.
But as I left I thought, what?
He's important.
I'm not important.
Why would you care about practicing with me?
That stuck with me all these years.
I was also a little disgusted sometimes by the residents of Green Gulch, because it turned out they were also ordinary human beings.
They would squabble and gossip.
It was mostly hidden from the practice period students, but I was around more and I started to be exposed to what really goes on.
I had two interactions with Yvonne Rand, who is a very important Western Zen teacher.
Pioneer.
I don't even know her whole story, but really a valuable teacher in the movement.
For whatever reason, my only two interactions with her were pretty negative.
It just makes me think it's just kind of happenstance, right?
Who we meet, when, and what they're doing and what their mood is.
I mostly toed the line and did what I was supposed to.
But by the end of the practice period I was a little tired of toeing the line and following all the rules.
So I was out in the garden playing my guitar, which you weren't supposed to do anywhere in the grounds.
They had this anti-music thing then.
Music was a distraction, and music shows up in the early Buddhist precepts as a distraction.
No music and dancing and stuff.
I think now they're a little lighter about this.
So interaction number one with Yvonne Rand was: "Excuse me, I'm doing a retreat here.
Do not play that guitar."
The other one was she got really upset with the farm manager.
Some decision he was making she felt had negative ecological repercussions on the valley, a beautiful little valley going down to the water.
I don't know what the details were, and she was probably right.
She was just yelling at this guy.
So it's funny, who knows who we'll encounter when, or what will be happening.
The whole time I was there I felt like, I don't really know if this is for me, but there's something here.
There's something to this.
And it felt like trying on a new suit of clothes, a different kind of clothes than you usually would wear.
I've never been terribly creative about the clothes I wear anyway.
And just kind of seeing, does this fit?
Maybe it fits.
It kind of fits.
A little tight in the shoulders or something.
But no, it looks good.
No, it doesn't look good.
I don't know.
Do I deserve these clothes?
Whose clothes are these?
When you're there in practice period, they ask you to stay in the valley and not go anywhere.
I think I cheated once and walked to town to get some candy or some dumb something.
But I figured since I was walking it was like a pilgrimage and it was okay.
It's surrounded by beautiful wild lands, ecologically somewhat denuded from their original state, I learned, but still beautiful.
And I didn't really know, have I learned anything?
Have I changed in some way?
Then I went to drive, I think to drive home for Christmas or something.
I got into my beat up ancient Toyota Corolla, which I bought for $400 as soon as I could manage to get a car.
My son isn't interested in driving.
He's now just about 16, but I got my license instantly and was saving for a car as soon as I could.
So I got into my Corolla, and the seats, I hadn't really noticed this, but the seats don't really go up.
People drive like this.
I sat down in the seat and I found myself sitting like this.
And it was the strangest moment.
I thought, is this the same car?
Everything looked different.
My whole perspective had changed.
So maybe I sort of learned something about sitting up straight.
When it was time to leave this first practice period for real, I was standing in line waiting to have lunch.
You'd line up, a buffet, wonderful food.
And Norman Fischer, whom I now knew a little bit, was behind me in line.
He taps me on the shoulder.
I turn around.
He says, "Excuse me, it's Tim, right?
Would you like to stay and work here?"
And I said, okay.
So then suddenly I wasn't leaving that day.
I stayed another three or four months working in the kitchen.
About a couple weeks later, I was asked to go to my first staff meeting.
It turned out they'd been having a lot of trouble over the last few years with young staff members.
People who looked like me, probably, basically seeing the work assignment as kind of like a free ride.
You get to live in this gorgeous place.
You didn't have to work that hard, maybe 25, 30 hours a week max.
And you get a little stipend, enough to go out for a beer once or something.
I think we got $60 or $70 a month or something like that.
Toothpaste, basically.
I think you got health insurance, too.
Anyway, they apparently had a lot of trouble with people like me not actually doing much Zen practice.
Just do your work and go goof off.
And who wouldn't?
Gorgeous place.
So they had concocted this practice agreement form.
You had to fill out a form.
Isn't that our first response to problems in the West?
Let's make a form.
So I'm looking at this form and puzzling over what to put down.
They didn't warn me about this form.
One of the things you had to put down was who is your practice leader.
They figured if you were in an assigned relationship with one of the teachers, you wouldn't goof off so much.
The person next to me was a woman named Fu Schroeder, who was the ino at the time.
Very impressive ino.
Really tough.
Very fierce.
If you slept in, she would come knock on your door: "Excuse me!
Time for zazen!"
And you would leap out of bed.
Somehow your clothes would be on and you'd be out the door in a minute and a half.
This happened once or twice to me and my roommates.
Of course, we weren't exactly going to bed when we were supposed to.
The wake-up bell was 4:20 or something like that. 4:40 maybe.
It was early.
But anyway, now I'm in a different role with Fu, the ino.
I'm sitting next to her as a fellow staff member, and suddenly she seems to be a little different person.
She says to me, "Put Norman down.
He's really easy."
So that was the beginning of my formal relationship with Norman Fischer.
And of course, that might as well have been what I would have picked anyway.
I would have just stayed there the rest of my life probably, trying to figure out if this suit of clothes fit or not.
I doubt I ever would have figured it out.
After a number of months, Norman again tapped me on the shoulder and said, "Excuse me, what's going on with you?
Weren't you taking some time off from school?
Do I remember right?"
I said, yeah, I remember right.
I was taking the year off from school.
But I don't know.
Why go back?
It's wonderful to be here and practice.
This is a lifetime commitment, right?
And he said, yeah, it's a lifetime commitment, and it's even better if you come back and do your lifetime commitment after you get your degree.
Please finish your degree.
So I finished my degree, and came back a couple years later to do another practice period, and again was leaving.
This time he didn't tell me to work in the kitchen.
I had more of a life then.
I had a job lined up doing botanical field surveys on the high slopes of Mount Rainier, which was kind of like my dream job.
I always thought the best thing in the world would be to get paid to be deep in the wilderness.
Yeah, I thought science was interesting too.
So maybe I wove that in there, but I don't think that was my real initial motivation.
I just wanted to be deep in the wilderness and get paid for it.
But Zen still didn't really feel like a very natural fit.
I appreciated it when I sat.
The days went better.
I was a little shy about it.
In my town of Santa Cruz, California, where I had gone to school, there was a small zendo about the size of this one, maybe a little smaller actually.
It was a very small sangha at the time.
I found out later that it was in an ebb, a sangha's ebb and flow.
This sangha had existed already for quite a number of years, but it was in an ebb.
Their teacher had left and there was no new teacher yet.
So there were only a couple of people there, and they would sit once or twice early in the morning, every day.
I think there was a weeknight, kind of like we have, with more people, but I didn't go to that.
In fact, I didn't really want to even talk to anybody.
I just wanted to sit down, do this Zen thing, and go on to school.
I don't think I particularly told any of my friends I was doing this either.
Maybe they noticed I always seemed to be at school before them.
I don't know, because I'd go on to college after finishing this Zen sitting at, I don't know what, 6 in the morning or 6:30, something like that.
Got a lot of studying done early in the morning.
But I didn't figure I could really keep this up without a place like that.
My understanding of Zen practice was that it's a place you go to.
There are people there, and once they ring that bell, you would be embarrassed to leave.
So you stick it out, you try to breathe.
There may be a lot of pain in your body or a lot of distracted thoughts, but whatever.
And then somehow the day goes better.
So when I was on my way to Mount Rainier, I went to see Norman and I said, well, thanks a lot.
I'm out, clocking out.
I want to punch my card out, because I was going somewhere with no Zen center.
He said, well, where are you going?
I said, Washington State.
And he said, that's funny.

I don't know if it was truly like the last week, but it was recently, sometime recently, a small group in Vancouver had invited him to start going up there to teach, to go and lead weekend retreats, stuff like that.
I still remember the way he said it.
He said, "Is that near Vancouver, Canada?"
And I said, yeah, that's near Vancouver, Canada.
Yeah, definitely.
He said, "Well, I'm going to go there.
Maybe you can come to a retreat there."
I said, okay.
Maybe I'm not checking out.
I didn't know.
The next thing I knew, I was living in Bellingham, even closer to Vancouver, Canada, and they were having a sesshin, I think the first residential sesshin that they had had there with Norman Fischer.
Was that like kind of a Boy Scout camp?
It wasn't called Boy Scouts, some other name.
There were so few people with experience, they immediately asked me to do all kinds of jobs, ring bells and stuff like that.
I think I was the timekeeper.
I remember Norman had a dear friend who died during that retreat.
That went on to be a theme.
I was with him many times when a dear friend died, or soon after a dear friend died.
In this case, it was a friend of his who practiced Tibetan Buddhism, who was doing the three-year retreat.
Do you know about the three-year retreats they do?
Sesshin's got nothing on these guys.
For three years, three months, and three days, they do meditation and study.
It's a little different structure.
All day, every day.
No days off.
You tend to do it mostly individually or in your own little room.
You come together for ceremonies and you go back to your own little room.
I don't think you see the teacher very often either.
So anyway, a friend of his, and they didn't really understand what had happened, but he was found suffocated against his meditation cushion.
Just something had happened.
I don't know if they ever figured out what, brain aneurysm or heart attack, but cause of death was suffocation.
So I soon realized this is not just fun and games.
Serious stuff is happening all the time.
At that retreat, I met a Bellingham resident named Florence Caplow, who turned out to be a botanist.
So suddenly we had all this stuff in common.
I was already on my way to being an ex-botanist, because to my great surprise, once I finally got out into the deep wilderness and was being paid for it, I didn't like it that much.
Like so isolating.
I was used to having all my Santa Cruz friends around and being able to go get organic vegetables and go to nice, sort of post-hippie community events.
And what's in the nearest town to where I was working?
One mini-mart, one lager bar, and maybe a laundromat.
The laundromat I think was further down the mountain.
So it wasn't the kind of culture I was used to.
I didn't quite adjust to that.
This is too isolating, darn it.
This turned out to be a theme of my whole life.
Okay, this is what I need to do.
This will be great.
This is everything I want.
And work hard for a few years, do a few more years of training, work your butt off trying to apply and make the right connections, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah.
And you get there, I get there, and realize, oh, this isn't working out.
This is what I wanted.
And Florence Caplow and I, and then soon Bob, here, and I reconnected, and started to realize, well, we could just sit together.
Norman encouraged us.
I remember his whole instruction on how to start this was, find a couple of friends and put a note up at the bookstore, and it'll work out.
It turned out to be true.

The three of us each had our different roles and energies, who would show up, who would not show up, who would call and say, I'm not showing up, but at least I know this is happening, and we were down unexpectedly for work, and we navigated that for a number of years.
And little by little, people came.
I remember one woman came right away.
She must have seen the note in the bookstore.
Came every week for months.
She was mourning her son, who had died of AIDS.
This was, the AIDS epidemic was still in full force then, 1991.
And then she went somewhere else.
People come, people go.
And then a year or two later, we had our first retreat, our first overnight retreat.
We just jumped into it.
We didn't just have a one-day sit or something like that.
We had our little weekly sitting, which was held in the fireplace room at the Fairhaven Library, probably for my convenience, since I lived a couple blocks up on Harris Street.
And then we said, let's have a retreat.
We'll have Norman Fischer come.
We'll find a place where we can all be.
And a buddy of ours offered his cabin on Lummi Island and his surrounding garden.
So we did it in the spring so we could camp out.
And somehow it was determined that Florence and I could start studying the precepts.
Then we would have Jukai in John Robinson's garden on a spring day in, I think, 1993.
I was looking for evidence, and I found a photo from 1993 of me, Florence, Norman, and another guy, John Wright, an early member.
And Norman looked so young.
He's younger than I am now.
He's in his mid-forties.
At the time I felt so grateful and impressed, and I still do, that Norman would come up.
He would end up coming up, between our group and the group in Vancouver, six times a year, year after year after year after year.
I don't know if we thought too much about what his other obligations might have been.
Like everyone, we're all a little self-centered, but we'd say, are you coming again?
He'd say, yep, I'm coming again.
And it would be kind of the same weekend.
Eventually we got a pattern going, which made it easier.
But occasionally it would occur to us, this is pretty impressive.
This wonderful teacher whom we're getting to know, and who is helping us make this whole thing real, constantly, somehow, is coming up from far away, so regularly, year after year.
But now I realize we were doing him a favor, too.
The situation he was within at San Francisco Zen Center was kind of top-heavy.
Lots of experienced people.
Not a lot of chances to teach, actually.
Plenty of administrative scut work to do, no doubt about that, but not a lot of opportunities to teach.
And so here we're offering him this wonderful opportunity to teach.
I mean, we must have been pretty fine, so eager.
We were pretty eager, what do you think?
Positive, we'd do anything.
He would often say, no, no, that's too much, and we'd say, no, no, no, we'll do it, we'll do it, and he'd say, no, no, that's too much, and we'd say, no, no, we'll do it.
Oryoki and stuff like that.
To this day, whenever we have oryoki, he says, oh, that's too hard, don't do oryoki.
No, no, no, we'll do it.
And I remember we had no resources here, of course, for sewing rakusu.
That was a total baffler.
So I went to Green Gulch to do that, stayed there for a week, working on it all day, every day.
And that was a mistake.
The guest manager wasn't really supposed to allow me to do that, but there was some kind of mix-up.
I was supposed to have been doing other work.
Eventually, towards the end of the week, somebody said to me, did they let you sew all day?
Yeah, yeah, you were supposed to spend the morning work period doing this other thing.
You've got to contribute.
Sorry.
Got pretty far in my rakusu, though.
And the day came, and of course the teacher picks names for you.
I think I didn't really totally understand, and I don't know if I'd ever been to anybody else's jukai ceremony.
I can't remember if there had been one at Green Gulch while I was there, and there might have been.
I certainly saw other ceremonies, the whole round of ceremonies that happens in a practice period, the shuso ceremonies, seasonal ceremonies.
I don't know if I'd seen a jukai.
So the name thing kind of snuck up on me.
In the middle of the ceremony, Norman is saying to me, and to Florence, Tim Burnett, your new name is, like, new name?
My new name was Nomon Do An.
And Florence's name changed with her priest ordination, so I can't remember what her original name was now.
Anyway, the name Nomon turned out to be kind of a strange name and a sweet name.
Norman's parents-in-law had been traveling in China, and they ran into a seal maker, who makes little chops, little seals that you seal documents with, dipped in red, pasty stuff.
And they said, oh, our son-in-law's, they met the seal maker who spoke a little English, and, oh, our son-in-law's a Buddhist priest.
I bet he could use a seal.
And the seal maker said, oh, what's his name?
And they said, Norman.
And of course, normally you would make the seal with your Buddhist name, which is based on Chinese characters.
In our case, Chinese characters pronounced in a Japanese fashion.
The way they pronounce Chinese characters in Japanese is different from how they pronounce them in Chinese, but that's another story.
Layers of language in this.
And so the seal maker just tried to figure out how the heck he could make Chinese characters that sounded like Norman.
Because "nor" is not really a sound in Chinese.
So he had to reach a little bit, and he found an unusual character which is pronounced no.
It's not normally used in a Dharma name.
And mon is the normal character for gate.
So this was Nomon, from Norman.
And so then Norman had this little seal and he didn't know what to do with it, because it was kind of useless to him.
It wasn't really his real name, his Dharma name.
So he gave it to me.
It was like a hand-me-down.
That's the best things are, really, right?
And wa and an, he picked out of the Dharma names book.
Wa means harmony, and an means peace.
And an shows up in lots of names, actually.
In temple names, too.
You'll hear an an.
And then we went on to have other jukais and just slowly, slowly, people come, people go.
We'd love each other.
We'd get mad at each other.
We'd get confused.
We didn't have a whole lot of context.
The bulk of the context that we had for this practice was my memory of what I'd done in Green Gulch an increasing number of years ago, and whatever Norman actually noticed that we were doing.
And he'd give us some suggestions.
Norman's style was never particularly to ask what we'd been doing, or to interfere in any way.
And I don't know if that's a deliberate strategy on his part, wanting to give us lots of room to grow and find our own way, or if he just didn't think of it, which is probably the latter.
Because when we were with him, we were doing something different than usual.
We'd be doing a retreat with a teacher in the middle of it.
And he would have some views about how we should do that.
But if we were doing something a little different than he thought, as often as not, I think he'd just let it go.
I can count on one hand the times that he actually grabbed me aside and said, you know what?
This is kind of wrong.
Very rare.
Mostly he just went with whatever was going on.

And we would notice from the way he comported himself and the way he moved around, what things he said, we would gradually, I think, harmonize more and more with the style of practice that he had learned at Zen Center.
And he himself had started to change.

One of the things that's been wonderful and a little bit challenging a few times, with Andrea and I working together these last weeks to prepare for this jukai ceremony, is that I knew that Norman had changed a number of things in our forms.
Mostly his orientation is to make things feel more inclusive, I think.
More accessible.
A little simpler.
He's always worried about the complexity of Zen.
And I think he's always been a little bit worried, actually, that people might misunderstand Zen practice as requiring a massive sort of temple infrastructure.
I think he's pretty critical of big sleeves.
I've heard him say something like the following many times.
And these are small.
This would be a little scandalous in a proper Soto temple.
They're supposed to go all the way to the floor when you stand.
Look at Andrea's.
I'm sure hers go to the floor.

So I remember him saying many times, the thing about these huge sleeves is what they do is they require you to have an entire infrastructure where everything's at this level so that the ordained people can operate.
So we're sitting on the floor, right?
And that's not traditional.
Traditional is we're on raised platforms.
Everything's raised up a little bit, so you never have to lower your arms.
You're just moving around like this.
I don't know what they had against lowering your arms down.
I don't know.
They don't do it.
So he wanted to simplify.
And so it's been interesting seeing ways of simplification that he did that I didn't actually even realize.
Little stuff, in a way.
But then depending on your ceremonial outlook, it could also look like big stuff.
For instance, towards the beginning of the Jukai ceremony, after you're all seated, the ordinees have not yet come in.
Andrea and I enter.
And at that point, according to the traditional ceremony, we're supposed to purify some water, make it into holy water, wisdom water, and purify the space before the ordinees come in.
Does that make sense?
They come into this purified place.
And then a little bit later, after they sit down, they get purified.
And then Norman skips the first part and does the purification of the room after they get here.
Just to make it easier, I suppose.
Andrea was shocked.
Not really shocked.
But you know what I mean.
Just like...
And I said, okay, let's purify the room earlier.
Beautiful.
We can add a little back in.
But we can also keep it simple and friendly.
And not worry too much.

What was great about going to Japan with Norman in 2010, with a bunch of other colleagues, was seeing that this message I'd been hearing more in San Francisco than here, this message of, this is the traditional way, this is the way they do it in Japan, you notice the article there?
We go to Japan and we go to a bunch of different temples and monasteries.
We see a plethora of different ways.
There's all kinds of different ways.
So there is a bit of a cult of purity that emerges in every practice, right?
Every religion.
And it's beautiful.
And we can appreciate it.
But it's also a little hampering.
And a little bit not quite literally true.
But it's okay.

I don't know how much to go into the early history, or we're at the end of the time that I allocated for the talk, but it's just wonderful that somehow, without really knowing what we were doing or having a master plan, and with lots of mistakes, and some real upsets, and lots of love too, somehow we're here today, in this space, preparing to do a jukai ceremony with two preceptors, three wonderful people.
And there's a really very real way that when people step forward to receive the precepts and commit to this life in this formal way, it helps all of us, it buoys all of us up.
We all take the precepts with them, we all receive the precepts with them.
I don't know if that phrase that we have in there, to give the precepts or to receive the precepts, totally makes sense.
How could there be something called precepts that we could give or receive?
Maybe life is nothing but precepts.
And this is a ceremony of remembering that.
So easily we forget that life is about precepts, and precepts ultimately are about love and forgiveness and being more intentional, more kind, more compassionate.
So maybe we should call it the precepts remembering ceremony, that would be a little more accurate.
But it's a deep kind of remembering.
And every one of us, just like me, brings a history to this moment, to this day.
Each of us with our own winding path.
And it's fun to do this practice of talking about your practice history.
Sometimes we call these way-seeking mind talks.
We should do this a little more often, I think.
And I know that the three ordinees got together with Andrea at her place and did short ones.
So it'd be wonderful if you'd share those with us here sometime.
What's great about it is it's different every time you tell it.
So is your history different?
Do you exactly remember your history?
Or are you just reinventing some past life of someone you barely know now?
So it's interesting.
So I was so amazed that people could practice for decades, but now that it's been 30 years longer, depending on how I count, it doesn't feel so impressive.
It just feels more ordinary.

One day at a time, one breath at a time, trying to sit every day, forgetting on more than a few days, getting sidetracked, remembering again, being deeply moved, deeply transformed, forgetting again, remembering again.
But the weird thing about it is this movement is still pretty young.
The people I was practicing with 30 years ago, not one of them could have practiced for 30 years, because there wasn't Zen in the West for 30 years then.
Think about that.
At least Zen that was very accessible to Western converts.
Of course there have been Zen priests and Zen practice for a hundred years, at least, since the first Japanese immigrants came.
But those two camps were so separate then, and still are a little more separate than I would like.
Doesn't seem to be any Japanese people here at the moment.
We have halfu.
Which is great.
That's a loan word they use in Japan.
They really say that, halfu.
Half and half.
Another one I love is if you and your friend wear the exact same clothes, that's matchingu.
Matching, matching, matchingu.
It's a great honor to be somebody's matchingu partner.
We're the exact same outfit.
So that's enough rambling for now.
And just to say thank you.
Really, as best I can.
Limited by my karmic conditioning and personality and all that.
As we all are.
But the beauty of it is that we can also see through that, can't we?
We can see the Buddha that's sitting here, that's sitting there, that's sitting everywhere.
So the ceremony of remembering the precepts is a ceremony of Buddha expressing herself.
Buddha expressing himself.
Nothing but Buddha.
Thank you.

verbatim.text: Good morning everybody. I'm pretty sure I first heard this poem by Mary Oliver from Norman many years ago. It continues to be a poem that I think about and share and recite all over the place. I got a little tired of it for a while and then I used it a bunch and people were so moved. Some things are so timeless. So Wild Geese by Mary Oliver. You know this poem? You don't have to be good. You don't have to walk on your knees through the desert for a hundred miles repenting. You only have to let the soft animal of your body love what it loves. Tell me about despair, yours, and I will tell you mine. Meanwhile, the world goes on. Meanwhile, the sun and the clear pebbles of the rain are moving across the landscapes,

over the prairies and the deep trees, the mountains and the rivers. Meanwhile, the wild geese, high in the clean blue air, are heading home again. Whoever you are, no matter how lonely, the world offers itself to your imagination. Calls to you like the wild geese, harsh and exciting, over and over announcing your place in the family of things. So anyway, 30 years ago, right now, some earlier version of me. The more you think about the statement like that, the more suspect it is, don't you think? Was that really me? Seems like it was me. Anyway, so we don't waste too much time on that. If you can actually tell the story, we'll say it was me.

I was at Green Gulch Farm about a month or maybe three weeks into the first residential training period that I sat there. I was 21 years old. The headteacher for the practice period was Dainian Ketagiri Roshi. He wasn't there the whole time though. He came and went a bit. I think he was also taking care of his sangha in Minnesota at the same time somehow. Tension Rev Anderson was kind of like the teacher on the ground that we saw every day. They were a group of, I don't know, 15, 16 practice period students. And we were mostly all pretty young. And I'm still in touch with a few of those people, lifelong friends. And so we went here and went there and got up and sat zazen and went to classes and did everything.

Norman Fischer was the director of Green Gulch and he would come and go a bit, interacting with us formally. I think just one evening a week he taught a class. I can't remember if it was on the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 lines or if it was on the Genjokoan. Genjokoan, thanks. I thought you might remember. Because I did two different practice periods and they blend together in my mind. But Bob appeared in somewhere in there. And I was really pretty impressed by all these great, worthy practitioners. I didn't really know their stories but it seemed like they must have been doing this forever.

Very dignified. What I understand in particular, then and now and probably until the day he dies, has this incredible grace and sort of shininess. It just kind of floats around through the space. Later on I had some judgmental feelings about that but I was also so impressed. As one does, right? Norman was a little more ordinary looking, crooked nose, you know, a little galumpy. So I was a little more comfortable with that.

I went to see, so this is not particularly in order. If I were to tell the whole story in order, we don't have enough time. But just impressions, you know, impressions. I went to see Norman towards the end of that first practice period. And in practice discussion he was not yet, hadn't yet received Dharma transmission. So it's called practice discussion just like it is here. When the teacher is not fully ordained yet. Are you hearing me okay? I'm not feeling like talking really loud.

You hear me okay? No? Not so much? You want to move up, Linda? I'll try to speak up a little bit. Anyway, I was so surprised at the end of this final interview. I forget where I was going next. Norman said, yeah. Norman said, well, I really appreciated practicing with you. And I think I just said, thanks.

But as I left I thought, what? I'm not, you know, he's important. I'm not important. Why would you care about practicing with me? That stuck with me all these years. I was also a little disgusted sometimes by the residents of Green Gulch. Because it turned out they were also ordinary human beings. And they would squabble and gossip.

It was mostly hidden from the practice period students. But I was around more and I started to be exposed to what really goes on. I had exactly two random thoughts. I had two interactions with Yvonne Rand who is a very important Western Zen teacher. Pioneer. I don't even know her whole story, but really valuable teacher in the movement. But for whatever reason my only two interactions with her were pretty negative. It just makes me think, you know, it's just kind of happenstance, right?

Who we meet, when and what they're doing and what their mood is. I mostly toed the line and did what I was supposed to. But by the end of the practice period I was a little tired of towing the line and following all the rules. And so I was out in the garden playing my guitar. Which you weren't supposed to do like anywhere in the grounds. They had this anti-music thing then. Music was a distraction. And music shows up in the early Buddhist precepts as a distraction.

No music and dancing and stuff. I think now they're a little lighter about this. So interaction number one with Yvonne Rand was, excuse me, I'm doing a retreat here. Do not play that guitar. The other one was she got really upset with the garden manager or the farm manager. She got upset with the farm manager. Some decision he was making she felt had negative ecological repercussions on the valley.

Beautiful little valley going down to the water. And I don't know what the details were and she was probably right. She was just yelling at this guy. So it's funny. Who knows who will encounter when or what will be happening. The whole time I was there I felt like, I don't really know if this is for me but there's something here. There's something to this.

And it felt like trying on a suit of clothes. Trying on a new suit of clothes. Different kind of clothes than you usually would wear. And I've never been terribly creative about the clothes I wear anyway. And just kind of seeing, does this fit? Maybe it fits. It kind of fits. You know, a little tight in the shoulders or something.

But no, it looks good. No, it doesn't look good. I don't know. Do I deserve these clothes? Whose clothes are these? When you're there in practice period they ask you to stay in the valley and not go anywhere. I think I cheated once and walked to town to get some candy or some dumb something. But I figured since I was walking it was like a pilgrimage and it was okay.

And it's surrounded by beautiful wild lands. Ecologically somewhat denuded from their original state, I learned, but still beautiful. And I didn't really know, you know, have I learned anything? Have I changed in some way? And then I went to drive, I think to drive home for Christmas or something. And I got into my beat up ancient Toyota Corolla, which I bought for $400 as soon as I could manage to get a car. My son isn't interested in driving. He's now just about 16, but I got my license instantly and was saving for a car as soon as I could.

So I got into my Corolla and the seats, I hadn't really noticed this, but the seats don't really go up. They kind of like, people drive like this. And I sat down in the seat and I found myself sitting like this. And it was the strangest moment. I thought, is this the same car? You know, like everything looked different. My whole perspective had changed. So maybe I sort of learned something about sitting up straight. When it was time to leave this first practice period for real, I was standing in line waiting to have lunch. You'd line up as buffet, wonderful food.

And Norman Fischer, you know how I now knew a little bit, was behind me in line. And he taps me on the shoulder. I turn around. He says, excuse me, it's Tim, right? Would you like to stay and work here? And I said, okay. So then suddenly I wasn't leaving that day. And I stayed another three or four months working in the kitchen. And about a couple weeks later, I was asked to go to my first staff meeting. And it turned out they'd been having a lot of trouble over the last few years with young staff members. People looked like me, probably.

Basically seeing the work assignment as kind of like a free ride. You get to live in this gorgeous place. You didn't have to work that hard. Maybe it was 25, 30 hours a week max. And you get a little stipend, you know, enough to go out for a beer once or something. I think we got $60 or $70 a month or something like that. Toothpaste, basically. I think you got health insurance, too. So anyway, but they had a lot of trouble apparently with people like me not actually doing much Zen practice. Just do your work and go goof off.

And who wouldn't? Gorgeous place. And so they had concocted this practice agreement form. You had to fill out a form. Isn't that our first? That's like our first response to problems in the West. Let's make a form. So I'm looking at this form and puzzling over what to put down. They didn't warn me about this form. And one of the things you had to put down was who is your practice leader? So they figured if you were in a kind of an assigned relationship with one of the teachers, you wouldn't goof off so much.

And the person next to me, a woman named Fu Schroeder, who was the Eno at the time. Very impressive Eno. Really tough. Very kind of fierce. If you slept in, she would come knock on your door. Excuse me! Time for Zazen! And you would leap out of bed. Somehow your clothes would be on and you'd be out the door in a minute and a half. This happened once or twice to me and my roommates. Of course we weren't exactly going to bed when we were supposed to.

And the wake-up bell was 420 or something like that. 440 maybe. It was early. But anyway, now I'm in a different role with Fu, the Eno. I'm sitting next to her as a fellow staff member. And suddenly she seems to be a little different person. And she says to me, put Norman down. He's really easy. So that was the beginning of my formal relationship with Norman Fischer. And of course, that might as well have been what I would have picked anyway.

I would have just stayed there the rest of my life probably. Trying to figure out if this suit of clothes fit or not. I doubt I ever would have figured it out. After a number of months, Norman again tapped me on the shoulder and says, Excuse me, what's going on with you? What's going on? And weren't you taking some time off from school? Do I remember right? I said, yeah, I remember right. I was taking the year off from school. But I don't know. Why go back?

It's wonderful to be here and practice. This is a lifetime commitment, right? And he said, yeah, it's a lifetime commitment. And it's even better if you come back and do your lifetime commitment after you get your degree. Please finish your degree. So I finished my degree. And came back a couple years later to do another practice period and again was leaving. This time he didn't tell me to work in the kitchen. I had more of a life then.

I had a job lined up. Doing field, botanical field surveys on the high slopes of Mount Rainier. Which was kind of like my dream job. I always thought the best thing in the world would be to get paid to be deep in the wilderness. Yeah, I thought science was interesting too. So maybe I wove that in there, but I don't think that was my real initial motivation. I just wanted to be deep in the wilderness and get paid for it. But Zen still didn't really feel like a very natural fit.

I appreciated it when I sat. The days went better. I was a little shy about it. In my town of Santa Cruz, where I had gone to school, Santa Cruz, California, there was a small Zen center. Zen to about the size of this one, maybe a little smaller actually. And it was a very small Sangha at the time. I found out later that it was in an ebb, Sangha's ebb and flow. This Sangha had existed already for quite a number of years, but it was in an ebb. Their teacher had left and there was no new teacher yet.

So there was only a couple of people there. And they would sit once or twice early in the morning, every day. And I think there was a weeknight, kind of like we have, with more people, but I didn't go to that. And in fact, I didn't really want to even talk to anybody. I just wanted to sit down, you know, do this Zen thing, and go on to school. I don't think I particularly told any of my friends I was doing this either. Maybe they noticed I always seemed to be at school before them. I don't know, you know, because I'd go on to college after finishing this Zen sitting at, I don't know what, 6 in the morning or 6.30, something like that.

Got a lot of studying done early in the morning. But I didn't figure I could really keep this up without a place like that. My understanding of Zen practice was it's a place you go to. And there are people there. And once they ring that bell, you would be embarrassed to leave. So you stick it out, you try to breathe. There may be a lot of pain in your body or a lot of distracted thoughts, but whatever. And then somehow the day goes better.

So when I was on my way to Mount Rainier, I went to see Norman and I said, well, thanks a lot. I'm out, you know, clocking out. I want to punch my card out because I was going somewhere with no Zen center. And I said, well, where are you going? I said, Washington State. And he said, that's funny. I don't know if it was truly like the last week, but it was recently, sometime recently. A small group in Vancouver had invited him to start going up there to teach, you know,

to go and lead weekend retreats, stuff like that. I still remember the way he said it. He said, is that near Vancouver, Canada? And I said, yeah, that's near Vancouver, Canada. Yeah, definitely. He said, well, I'm going to go there. Maybe you can come to a retreat there. I said, OK.

Maybe I'm not checking out. I didn't know. The next thing I knew, I was living in Bellingham, even closer to Vancouver, Canada, and they were having a sesshin. I think the first residential sesshin that they had had there with Norman Fischer. Was that like kind of a Boy Scout camp? It wasn't called Boy Scouts, some other name. And there were so few people with experience, they immediately asked me to do all kinds of jobs,

ring bells and stuff like that. I think I was the timekeeper. And I remember Norman had a dear friend who died during that retreat. And that went on to be a theme. I was with him many times when a dear friend died, or soon after a dear friend died. In this case, it was a friend of his who practiced Tibetan Buddhism, who was doing the three-year retreat. Do you know about the three-year retreats they do?

Sesshin and nothing on these guys. For three years, three months, and three days, they do meditation and study. It's a little different structure. All day, every day. No days off. You tend to do it mostly individually or in your own little room. You come together for ceremonies and you go back to your own little room. I don't think you see the teacher very often either.

So anyway, a friend of his, and they didn't really understand what had happened, but he was found like suffocated against his meditation cushion. Just something had happened. I don't know if they ever figured out what brain aneurysm or heart attack, but cause of death was suffocation. So I soon realized this is not just fun and games, you know. Serious stuff is happening all the time. At that retreat, I met a Bellingham resident named Florence Caplow,

who turned out to be a botanist. So suddenly we had all this stuff in common. I was already on my way to being an ex-botanist, because to my great surprise, once I finally got out into the deep wilderness and was being paid for it, I didn't like it that much. Like so isolating. I was used to having all my Santa Cruz friends around

and being able to go get organic vegetables and go to nice, you know, sort of post-hippie community events. And what's in the nearest town to where I was working? One mini-mart, one lager bar, and maybe a laundromat. You know, the laundromat I think was further down the mountain. So it wasn't the kind of culture I was used to. I didn't quite adjust to that. This is too isolating, darn it.

This turned out to be a theme of my whole life. Okay, this is what I need to do. This will be great. This is everything I want. And work hard for a few years, do a few more years of training, work your butt off trying to apply and make the right connections, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah.

And you get there, I get there, and realize, oh, this isn't working out. This is what I wanted. And Florence Caplow and I, and then soon Bob, here and I reconnected, started to realize, well, we could just sit together. Norman encouraged us. I remember his whole instruction on how to start this was,

find a couple of friends and put a note up at the bookstore, and it'll work out. It turned out to be true. The three of us each kind of had our different roles and energies, you know, who would show up, who would not show up, who would call and say, I'm not showing up, but at least I know this is happening, and we were down unexpectedly for work,

and, you know, we kind of navigated that for a number of years. And little by little, people came. I remember one woman came right away. She must have seen the note in the bookstore. Came every week for months. She was mourning her son, who had died of AIDS. And this was, you know, the AIDS epidemic was still full force then, 1991.

And then she went somewhere else. People come, people go. And then a year or two later, we had our first retreat, our first, you know, overnight retreat. We just kind of jumped into it. We didn't just have like a one-day sit or something like that. We had our just little weekly sitting, which was held in the fireplace room at the Fairhaven Library,

probably for my convenience, since I lived a couple blocks up on Harris Street. And then we said, let's have a retreat. We'll have Norman Fischer come. We'll find a place where we can all be. And a buddy of ours offered his cabin on Lummi Island and his surrounding garden. So we did in the spring so we could camp out.

And somehow it was determined that Florence and I could start studying the precepts. Then we would have Jukai in John Robinson's garden on a spring day in, I think, 1993. I was looking for evidence, and I found a photo from 1993 of me, Florence, Norman, and another guy, John Wright, was an early member.

And Norman looked so young. And he's younger than I am now. He's in his mid-forties. And at the time I felt so grateful and impressed, you know, and I still do, that Norman would come up and he would end up coming up between our group and the group in Vancouver. He would end up coming up six times a year,

year after year after year after year. I don't know if we thought too much about what his other obligations might have been. Like everyone, we're all a little self-centered, but we'd say, are you coming again? He'd say, yep, I'm coming again. And it would be kind of the same weekend. Eventually we got a pattern going, which made it easier.

But occasionally it would occur to us, this is pretty impressive. This wonderful teacher whom we're getting to know and is helping us make this whole thing real, like constantly, somehow, is coming up from far away, so regularly, year after year. But now I realize we were doing him a favor, too. The situation he was within

at San Francisco Zen Center was kind of top-heavy. Lots of experienced people. Not a lot of chances to teach, actually. Plenty of administrative scut work to do, no doubt about that, but not a lot of opportunities to teach. And so here we're offering him this wonderful opportunity, actually, to teach.

I mean, we must have been pretty fine, so eager, you know. We were pretty eager, what do you think? Positive, you know, we'd do anything. He would often say, no, no, that's too much, and we'd say, no, no, no, we'll do it, we'll do it, and he'd say, no, no, that's too much, ah, no, no, we'll do it, you know.

Oryoki and stuff like that. To this day, whenever we have oryoki, he says, oh, that's too hard, don't do oryoki. No, no, no, we'll do it, you know. And I remember we had no resources here, of course, for sewing rakusu. That was a total baffler. So I went to Green Gulch to do that,

stayed there for a week, working on it like all day, every day. And that was a mistake. The guest manager wasn't really supposed to allow me to do that, but there was some kind of mix-up. I was supposed to have been doing other work. Eventually, towards the end of the week, somebody said to me, did they let you sew all day?

Yeah, yeah, you were supposed to spend the morning work period doing this other thing. You know, you've got to contribute. Sorry. Got pretty far in my rakusu, though. And the day came, and of course the teacher picks names for you. I think I didn't really totally understand,

and I don't know if I'd ever been to anybody else's jukai ceremony. I can't remember if there had been one at Green Gulch while I was there, and there might have been. I certainly saw other ceremonies, you know, the whole round of ceremonies that happens in a practice period,

the shuso ceremonies, seasonal ceremonies that happen. I don't know if I'd seen a jukai. So the name thing kind of snuck up on me, you know. In the middle of the ceremony, Norman is saying to me, and to Florence, you know, Tim Burnett, your new name is, like, new name?

My new name was No Man Do An. And Florence's name changed with her priest ordination, so I can't remember what her original name was now. Anyway, the name No Man turned out to be kind of a strange name and a sweet name.

Norman's parents-in-law had been traveling in China, and they ran into a seal maker, you know, who makes little chops, little seals that you seal documents with, dip them in red, pasty stuff. And they said,

oh, you know, our son-in-law's, you know, they met the seal maker who spoke a little English, and oh, our son-in-law's a Buddhist priest. I bet he could use a seal. And the seal maker said, oh, what's his name? And they said, Norman. And of course, normally you would make the seal

with your Buddhist name, which actually has Chinese, which is based on Chinese characters. In our case, Chinese characters pronounced in a Japanese fashion. The Japanese way they pronounce Chinese characters was a different way they pronounce them in Japanese, but that's another story.

Layers of language in this. And so the seal maker just tried to figure out how the heck he could make Chinese characters that sounded like Norman. Because nor is not really a sound in Chinese. So he had to reach a little bit, and he found an unusual character
which is pronounced noul. It's not normally used in a Dharma name. And moul is the normal character for gate. So this was Nomon, was from noulman.

And so then Norman had this little seal and he didn't know what to do with it, because it was kind of useless to him. You know, it wasn't really his real name, his Dharma name. So he gave it to me. It was like a hand-me-down. That's the best things are, really, right?
And thou and an, he picked out of the Dharma names book. Thou means harmony, and an means peace. And an shows up in lots of names, actually. In temple names, too. You'll hear an an.

And then we went on to have other jukais and just kind of slowly, slowly, you know, people come, people go. We'd love each other. We'd get mad at each other. We'd get confused. We didn't have a whole lot of context. The bulk of the context that we had for this practice

was my memory of what I'd done in Green Gulch an increasing number of years ago. And whatever Norman actually noticed that we were doing. And he'd give us some suggestions. Norman's style was never particularly to ask what we'd been doing. Or kind of interfere

in any way. And I don't know if that's a deliberate strategy in his part of wanting to give us lots of room to grow and kind of find our own way. Or if he just didn't think of it, you know. Which is probably the latter. Because when we were with him, we were doing

something different than usual. We'd be doing a retreat with a teacher in the middle of it. And he would have some views about how we should do that. But if we were doing something a little different than he thought, as often as not, I think he'd just let it go. I can count in one hand the times that he actually kind of grabbed me aside

and said, you know what? This is kind of wrong. Very rare. Mostly he just went with whatever was going on. And we would kind of notice from his the way he comported himself and the way he moved around. What things he said.

We would gradually, I think, sort of harmonize more and more with the style of practice that he had learned at Zen Center. And that he himself had started to change. One of the things that's been wonderful and a little bit challenging a few times with Andrea and I

working together these last weeks to prepare for this jukai ceremony is I knew that Norman had changed a number of things in our forum. Mostly his orientation is to make things feel more inclusive, I think. More accessible.

A little simpler. He's always worried about the complexity of Zen. And I think he's always kind of been a little bit worried actually that people might misunderstand Zen practice as requiring a massive sort of temple infrastructure. I think he's pretty critical of big sleeves.

I've heard him say something like the following many times. And these are small. This would be a little scandalous in a proper Soto temple. They're supposed to go all the way to the floor when you stand. Look at Andrea's. I'm sure hers go to the floor. So I remember him saying many times, the thing about these huge sleeves

is what they do is they require you to have an entire infrastructure where everything's at this level so that the ordained people can operate. So we're sitting on the floor, right? And that's not traditional. Traditional is we're on raised platforms. Everything's raised up a little bit.

So you never have to lower your arms. You're just moving around like this. I don't know what they had against lowering your arms down. I don't know. They don't do it. So he wanted to simplify. And so it's been interesting seeing ways of simplification that he did that I didn't actually even realize.

Little stuff, in a way. But then depending on your ceremonial outlook, it could also look like big stuff. For instance, towards the beginning of the Jukai ceremony, after you're all seated, the ordinees have not yet come in.
Andrea and I enter. And at that point, according to the traditional ceremony, we're supposed to purify some water, make it into holy water, wisdom water, and purify the space

before the ordinees come in. Does that make sense? They come into this purified place. And then a little bit later, after they sit down, they get purified. And then Norman skips the first part and does the purification of the room after they get here.
Just to make it easier, I suppose. Andrea was shocked. Not really shocked. But you know what I mean. Just like... And I said, okay, let's purify the room earlier. Beautiful.

Beautiful. We can add a little back in. But we can also keep it simple and friendly. And not worry too much. What was great about going to Japan with Norman in 2010, with a bunch of other colleagues, was seeing that this message I'd been hearing

more in San Francisco than here, this message of, this is the traditional way. This is the way they do it in Japan. You notice the article there? We go to Japan and we go to a bunch of different temples and monasteries. We see a plethora of different ways.

There's all kinds of different ways. So there is a bit of a cult of purity that emerges in every practice, right? Every religion. And it's beautiful. And we can appreciate it. But it's also a little hampering. And a little bit

not quite literally true. But it's okay. I don't know how much to go into the early history or we're at the end of the time that I allocated for the talk, but it's just wonderful that somehow, without really knowing what we were doing or having a master plan
or and with lots of mistakes, you know, and some real upsets, you know, and lots of love too. Somehow we're here today, in this space, praying to do a jukai ceremony with

two preceptors, three wonderful people. And there's a way too, a really very real way that when people step forward to receive the precepts and commit to this life in this formal way, it helps all of us, you know, it boys all of us up.

We all take the precepts with them, we all receive the precepts with them. I don't know if, you know, that phrase that we have in there, to give the precepts or to receive the precepts, I don't know if it totally makes sense though. How could there be a something called precepts that we could give or receive?
Maybe life is nothing but precepts. And this is a ceremony of remembering that. So easily we forget that life is about precepts and precepts ultimately are about love and forgiveness

and being more intentional, more kind, more compassionate. So maybe we should call it the precepts remembering ceremony, that would be a little more accurate. But it's a deep kind of remembering. And every one of us, just like me, brings a history to this moment, to this day. Each of us with our own winding path.

And it's fun to do this practice of talking about your practice history. Sometimes we call this way seeking mind talks. We should do this a little more often, I think. And I know that the three Ordinese got together with Andrew at her place and did short ones. So it'd be wonderful if you'd share those with us here sometime.

What's great about it is it's different every time you tell it. So is your history different? Do you exactly remember your history? Or are you just reinventing some past life of someone you barely know now? So it's interesting.

So I was so amazed that people could practice for decades, but now that it's been 30 years longer, depending on how I count, it doesn't feel so impressive. It just feels more ordinary. One day at a time, one breath at a time, trying to sit

every day, forgetting on more than a few days, getting sidetracked, remembering again, being deeply moved, deeply transformed, forgetting again, remembering again. But the weird thing about it is this movement is still pretty young. The people I was practicing

with 30 years ago, not one of them could have practiced for 30 years, because there wasn't Zen in the West for 30 years then. Think about that. At least Zen that was very accessible to Western converts. Of course there have been Zen priests and Zen practice for a hundred years, at least, since the first

Japanese immigrants came. But those two camps were so separate then, and still are a little more separate than I would like. Doesn't seem to be any Japanese people here at the moment. We have halfu. Which is great. That's a loan word they use

in Japan. They really say that, halfu. Half and half. Another one I love is if you and your friend wear the exact same clothes, that's matchingu. Matching, matching, matchingu. It's a great honor to be somebody's matchingu partner. We're the exact same
